boii-400.t: Celtic people who settled the plain around Bologna around 400 BCE and fought Rome for two centuries before being defeated in 191 BCE.
boii-400.o: The Boii crossed the Alps into the Po valley around 400 BCE, part of the great Celtic migration into Italy. They settled the plain south of the Po in modern Emilia, taking over the Etruscan city of Felsina, which became Bononia. Other Boii lived north of the Alps in Bohemia, which bears their name.
boii-400.r: The Cisalpine Boii were organised in many clans under chiefs, living in villages and small towns and farming the rich plain; they raised pigs and grain. Polybius describes their warrior elites, whose wealth lay in cattle and gold. Together with the Insubres they were the main Gaulish power in Italy, fighting Rome at Telamon in 225 BCE.
boii-400.e: In 218 BCE they attacked Rome's new colonies at Placentia and Cremona and supported Hannibal; in 216 BCE they ambushed and killed the consul-elect Postumius. Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated them in 191 BCE and confiscated half their land, and Rome founded Bononia in 189 BCE.

boii.t: A powerful Celtic people of central Europe whose name survives in 'Bohemia', builders of large fortified towns before Dacian and Germanic pressure broke them.
boii.o: The Boii were a Celtic people of the La Tène culture who appear in written sources from the 4th century BCE. One branch settled in the Po valley of northern Italy, where it fought Rome until defeated in 191 BCE; another held Bohemia and spread along the Danube into what is now Austria, Slovakia and western Hungary.
boii.r: Like other late Celtic peoples, the Boii lived in a world of chieftains, warrior elites and druids. They built oppida, large fortified towns such as Závist near Prague and the settlement at Bratislava, where they minted silver coins, some bearing the name Biatec. Ironworking, glass bracelets and long-distance trade with the Mediterranean world marked their prosperity in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.
boii.e: Around 60 BCE the Boii were crushed by the Dacian king Burebista, and part of the people joined the Helvetii in their failed migration of 58 BCE. Germanic Marcomanni later occupied Bohemia, but the Latin name Boiohaemum, 'home of the Boii', lives on as Bohemia, and possibly in Bavaria.

bituriges-cubi.t: Powerful Gallic people of Berry whose capital Avaricum, modern Bourges, was stormed by Caesar in one of the bloodiest sieges of the Gallic War.
bituriges-cubi.o: The Bituriges, whose name means 'kings of the world', occupied the middle Loire and Cher basins around Avaricum (Bourges). Livy tells a legend that in the 6th century BCE their king Ambigatus held supremacy over the Celts and sent his nephews Bellovesus and Segovesus to lead migrations into Italy and the Hercynian Forest. A related branch, the Bituriges Vivisci, later settled at Bordeaux.
bituriges-cubi.r: Their land was rich in iron ore, and the Bituriges were renowned smiths and metalworkers. Avaricum, defended by a massive timber-laced murus gallicus rampart, was one of the largest and wealthiest oppida in Gaul.
bituriges-cubi.e: In 52 BCE they joined Vercingetorix and burned some twenty of their own towns to starve the Romans, but spared Avaricum, which Caesar took after a hard siege, killing most of its inhabitants. Under Rome their territory became a civitas of Aquitania, the origin of the province of Berry.

barony-of-arcadia.t: Barony in the south-western Peloponnese around the castle of Arcadia (Kyparissia), the last refuge of the last prince of Achaea.
barony-of-arcadia.o: Arcadia, the medieval name of Kyparissia, was one of the domains held by the Villehardouin family after the conquest of the Morea, together with Kalamata, and was organised as a barony of the Principality of Achaea in the early 13th century.
barony-of-arcadia.r: The barony centred on the coastal castle above Kyparissia and its fertile surroundings, and was held by a succession of Frankish families, among them the Le Maure. In the late 14th century it passed to the Genoese Zaccaria family through Andronikos Asen Zaccaria, whose son Centurione II Zaccaria became Prince of Achaea in 1404.
barony-of-arcadia.e: As the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea conquered the rest of the principality, Centurione II retreated to Arcadia. After his death in 1432 Thomas Palaiologos took it over, ending Latin rule in the region.

british-cyprus.t: Cyprus under British rule from 1878 to 1960, a strategic base whose Greek Cypriot campaign for union with Greece led to independence.
british-cyprus.o: By the Cyprus Convention of 1878, the Ottoman Empire allowed Britain to occupy and administer Cyprus, while keeping formal sovereignty, in return for British support against Russia. Sir Garnet Wolseley became the first high commissioner. Britain annexed the island when the Ottomans entered the First World War in 1914 and made it a crown colony in 1925.
british-cyprus.r: A British governor ruled with a partly elected legislative council, abolished after the 1931 riots, when Government House was burned. The population, about four-fifths Greek Orthodox and one-fifth Turkish Muslim, was divided by the Greek demand for enosis, union with Greece. Agriculture, mining and later British military bases shaped the economy.
british-cyprus.e: From 1955 the EOKA guerrilla movement under George Grivas, backed by Archbishop Makarios III, fought British rule. The Zurich and London agreements of 1959 created the Republic of Cyprus, which became independent in August 1960, with Britain keeping two sovereign base areas.

bituriges-vivisci.t: Offshoot of the Bituriges settled on the Gironde estuary, whose trading port of Burdigala grew into Bordeaux.
bituriges-vivisci.o: Strabo notes that the Bituriges Vivisci were the only Celtic people living among the Aquitani, which suggests they migrated from the Bituriges Cubi of Berry to the lower Garonne, perhaps in the 3rd or 2nd century BCE. Their emporium Burdigala stood on a bend of the Garonne.
bituriges-vivisci.r: Burdigala was a trading port linking the Atlantic with the Mediterranean by the Garonne and Aude route, handling tin, metals and Italian wine. Caesar does not name them, perhaps because they did not resist him.
bituriges-vivisci.e: Under Rome Burdigala became the capital of Aquitania and a rich city whose vineyards, based on a vine named Biturica after the people, laid the foundations of the Bordeaux wine trade. The poet Ausonius was born there in the 4th century.

boii-of-gaul.t: Band of Boii who joined the Helvetian migration of 58 BCE and were resettled by Caesar in Aeduan territory.
boii-of-gaul.o: The Boii were a widespread Celtic people known in Bohemia, which takes its name from them, and in northern Italy. Caesar records that thirty-two thousand Boii joined the Helvetii in 58 BCE after besieging Noricum.
boii-of-gaul.r: After the defeat of the Helvetii near Bibracte, the Aedui asked Caesar to let the Boii settle in their land because of their courage. They received the town of Gorgobina, perhaps near Saint-Parize-le-Châtel.
boii-of-gaul.e: In 52 BCE Vercingetorix besieged Gorgobina to punish them for their loyalty to Rome, and Caesar marched to their relief. They later vanish as a separate group within the Aeduan civitas.

baiocasses.t: Gallic people of the Bessin in Normandy whose town Augustodurum grew into Bayeux.
baiocasses.o: Known from Pliny and later Roman sources, the Baiocasses lived along the Calvados coast west of the Orne. In Caesar's day they were probably counted among the Armorican peoples.
baiocasses.r: No rulers or pre-Roman institutions are recorded.
baiocasses.e: Under Rome their chief town was Augustodurum, renamed Baiocasses in late antiquity, the origin of Bayeux. It became a bishopric, and in the 11th century the Bayeux Tapestry was made for its cathedral.

bergistani.t: A small Iberian people of the Catalan pre-Pyrenees whose repeated revolts against Cato in 195 BCE ended in their enslavement.
bergistani.o: The Bergistani lived in the upper Llobregat valley of central Catalonia, a region still called the Berguedà after them. They were an Iberian-speaking hill people whose main stronghold was the fortress of Bergium, perhaps near modern Berga.
bergistani.r: Little is known about their society beyond Livy's narrative. They lived from mixed farming and herding in a mountainous district and defended themselves from fortified hilltops.
bergistani.e: In 195 BCE they rose twice against the consul Cato. After the second revolt he took their strongholds and sold the inhabitants into slavery, and Bergium itself fell when its exiled leader helped the Romans inside. The territory was absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

breuci.t: Pannonian people of the lower Sava valley who led, and then betrayed, the great revolt against Rome of 6–9 CE.
breuci.o: The Breuci lived along the lower Sava in modern Croatia, Bosnia and Serbia, among the Pannonian peoples of the region. They appear in Roman sources from the 2nd century BCE, when Roman armies first pushed into the Sava valley.
breuci.r: Known mainly from Roman accounts, they were a populous tribal people of farmers and stockbreeders, said to field large armies. In 6 CE, when Rome levied troops for a war against the Marcomanni, they rose under Bato the Breucian and Pinnes, joining the Daesitiates in the Great Illyrian Revolt.
breuci.e: In 8 CE Bato the Breucian surrendered Pinnes to Rome and was then executed by Bato of the Daesitiates. The Breuci submitted, and their young men were enrolled in Roman auxiliary units, the cohortes Breucorum, that served across the empire.

belgae-britain.t: Central southern British people around Winchester, whose name recalls the Belgae of northern Gaul and who formed a civitas of Roman Britain.
belgae-britain.o: Caesar wrote that the coastal parts of Britain had been settled by Belgae from Gaul who kept their tribal names, and Belgic coins circulated widely in the south from the 2nd century BCE. A people called Belgae is named only from Roman times, however, and their pre-conquest identity is uncertain; Winchester, the later Venta Belgarum, had a late Iron Age enclosure at Oram's Arbour.
belgae-britain.r: Before the conquest the region of Hampshire and Wiltshire seems to have fallen within the sphere of the Atrebates (Britain) and their kings Commius, Tincomarus and Verica, sharing their coinage and links with Gaul. Farming was rich on the chalk downs, and hillforts such as Danebury had been major storage centres in earlier centuries.
belgae-britain.e: After 43 the area may first have been part of the realm of Togidubnus in the Kingdom of the Regni. On his death it was organised as the civitas of the Belgae, with Venta Belgarum as its capital; Ptolemy also lists Aquae Sulis, Bath, among their towns. Winchester later became the royal seat of Wessex.

bonapartist-spain.t: The Spanish kingdom of Joseph Bonaparte, imposed by Napoleon in 1808 and swept away by the Peninsular War.
bonapartist-spain.o: In 1808 Napoleon summoned Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII to Bayonne and forced both to abdicate. He gave the throne to his brother Joseph, who was proclaimed Joseph I and granted the Statute of Bayonne, Spain's first constitution, while the Madrid rising of 2 May was brutally suppressed.
bonapartist-spain.r: Joseph's government, supported by reformist afrancesados, abolished the Inquisition, seigneurial rights and many convents. But it depended entirely on French armies and never controlled the whole country. Patriot juntas, the Cortes of Cádiz with its Constitution of 1812, guerrillas and Wellington's Anglo-Portuguese army fought it throughout the Peninsular War.
bonapartist-spain.e: After the defeat at Vitoria in June 1813 Joseph left Spain. By the Treaty of Valençay in December 1813 Napoleon restored Ferdinand VII, returning the country to Bourbon Spain.

barony-of-akova.t: Frankish barony in the hills of western Arcadia, centred on the castle the French called Matagrifon, lost to the Byzantines in 1320.
barony-of-akova.o: The barony of Akova was among the twelve original baronies of the Principality of Achaea, created around 1209 and granted to Walter of Rosieres, with 24 knight's fiefs. Its castle in the mountains between Elis and Arcadia was called Matagrifon, 'kill the Greeks', reflecting its role in holding down the region.
barony-of-akova.r: The barons owed service to the prince and sat in his high court. After the Rosieres line died out, the inheritance of Margaret of Passavant to Akova was disputed in the 1270s, a famous case recorded in the Chronicle of the Morea and in the Assizes of Romania, and much of the barony passed to the princely domain.
barony-of-akova.e: In 1320 the Byzantine governor Andronikos Asen captured Akova along with Karytaina and other castles of central Peloponnese, bringing the barony into what became the Despotate of the Morea.

bellovaci.t: The most powerful of the Belgic peoples, around Beauvais, who fought Caesar in 57 BCE and led one of the last Gallic revolts in 51 BCE.
bellovaci.o: The Bellovaci lived in the modern Oise and Picardy around Beauvais. Caesar was told that they could field a hundred thousand men and had promised sixty thousand to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
bellovaci.r: Their society was led by a warrior nobility, and they had ties to the Aedui. Large sanctuaries such as Gournay-sur-Aronde, with displays of weapons and sacrificed animals, show their religious practice.
bellovaci.e: In 57 BCE they surrendered at Bratuspantium after the Aeduan Diviciacus spoke for them. In 51 BCE they rose under Correus, who died fighting. Under Rome their chief town became Caesaromagus, later Beauvais.

barony-of-karytaina.t: Frankish barony in the mountains of central Peloponnese, guarded by the castle of Karytaina and celebrated through its lord Geoffrey of Bruyeres in the Chronicle of the Morea.
barony-of-karytaina.o: The barony of Karytaina, also called Skorta after its mountainous district, was created around 1209 in the Principality of Achaea and granted to Hugh of Bruyeres. With 22 knight's fiefs it was one of the largest baronies, set to control the unruly highlands of the upper Alpheios valley.
barony-of-karytaina.r: Hugh's son Geoffrey of Bruyeres built the castle of Karytaina on a crag above the Alpheios around 1254. He was the model knight of the Chronicle of the Morea, admired for his courage despite rebelling against Prince William II and eloping with a vassal's wife. Greek villagers and local archons held land under the barons.
barony-of-karytaina.e: After Geoffrey died in 1275 without a male heir, half the barony reverted to the prince and its fortunes declined. In 1320 Andronikos Asen, the Byzantine governor of Mistras, took Karytaina and much of Skorta, ending Frankish rule there.

batavi.t: Germanic people of the Rhine delta who served as Rome's elite soldiers and imperial bodyguards, then rose in a great revolt in 69 CE.
batavi.o: Tacitus says the Batavi were a branch of the Chatti who, after a quarrel at home, settled on the island between the Rhine and the Waal, the modern Betuwe in the Netherlands, probably in the later 1st century BCE.
batavi.r: Instead of paying tribute, they supplied Rome with soldiers: cavalry famous for swimming rivers in full armour, auxiliary cohorts and the emperors' German bodyguard. Their noble families commanded these units, and their chief town Batavodurum stood at Nijmegen.
batavi.e: In 69 CE Julius Civilis led a revolt joined by the Cananefates, Frisii and Treveri, which was crushed in 70 CE. The Batavi resumed service, and Ulpia Noviomagus (Nijmegen) became a Roman town. They faded in the Frankish period, but the Dutch long saw them as ancestors.

berones.t: A Celtic people of the upper Ebro in La Rioja, whose towns Vareia, Tritium and Libia lay on the routes into the Meseta.
berones.o: The Berones lived in the upper Ebro valley, in modern La Rioja, from about the 4th century BCE. Strabo described them as Celts, and their neighbours were the Autrigones, Pellendones and Vascones.
berones.r: Little is known of their government. Their towns included Vareia near Logroño, Tritium and Libia, and they lived from farming the fertile Ebro valley and herding. They reportedly served as mercenaries in conflicts of the 2nd century BCE.
berones.e: They came under Roman control in the 2nd century BCE during the Celtiberian wars. In 76 BCE Sertorius captured Vareia during his war against Rome. The Berones were absorbed into Hispania Citerior, and Tritium Magallum became a major Roman pottery centre.

bailiwick-of-guernsey.t: A self-governing British Crown Dependency of Channel Islands, held by the crown as heir of the Dukes of Normandy since 1204.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.o: Guernsey belonged to the Duchy of Normandy from the 10th century. When King John lost continental Normandy to Philip II of France in 1204, the islands stayed with the English crown, and a separate bailiwick, under its own bailiff and royal court, developed for Guernsey, Alderney, Sark and the smaller islands.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.r: Guernsey kept Norman customary law, its Royal Court of jurats and, later, the States of Deliberation as its parliament. Its economy rested on fishing, knitting, privateering and later tomatoes, horticulture and finance. Saint Peter Port was a major harbour. During the English Civil War it sided with Parliament, and Victor Hugo lived there in exile from 1855.
bailiwick-of-guernsey.e: Guernsey was occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency, not part of the United Kingdom, with its own government, laws and taxes, while the UK handles defence and international relations.

balearic-islanders.t: The tower-building peoples of Mallorca and Menorca, whose stone talaiots and taulas still dot the islands and whose slingers fought for Carthage and Rome.
balearic-islanders.o: From around 1000 BCE the islanders of Mallorca and Menorca developed what archaeologists call the Talaiotic culture, named after the talaiots, massive dry-stone towers that dominated fortified villages. It grew out of the earlier Naviform culture of boat-shaped houses and stone tombs such as the Naveta des Tudons on Menorca.
balearic-islanders.r: There was no single state: the islands were divided among village communities, probably led by local chiefs, living from herding, farming and some trade with Phoenician and Punic merchants, especially from nearby Ebusus. Menorca's T-shaped taulas stood in sanctuary enclosures. The islanders were famed throughout the Mediterranean as slingers and served as mercenaries in Carthaginian armies, including Hannibal's.
balearic-islanders.e: Accused of sheltering pirates, the islands were conquered in 123 BCE by the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus, who took the name Balearicus and founded the towns of Palma and Pollentia. Talaiotic traditions faded under Roman rule, but hundreds of monuments survive.

bessi.t: Thracian highland people of the Rhodopes and Haemus, keepers of a famous oracle of Dionysus and stubborn rebels against Rome.
bessi.o: Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BCE, names the Bessi as the priests of the oracle of Dionysus in the mountains of the Satrae. By later centuries they were a distinct people of the upper Hebrus (Maritsa) and Rhodope ranges in modern Bulgaria.
bessi.r: A loose tribal people of mountain country, the Bessi combined herding, mining and raiding. Their religious standing as guardians of the Dionysian sanctuary gave them prestige among Thracians. They clashed with the Odrysian Kingdom and with Macedon, and later raided Roman Macedonia.
bessi.e: Marcus Licinius Crassus subdued them in 29 BCE, but in 11 BCE the priest Vologases led a major revolt that took years to crush. Their name survived under Rome, and a Bessian language was reportedly still used in monastic worship in the 6th century CE.

bructeri.t: A Germanic people of Westphalia who fought Rome alongside Arminius and sheltered the seeress Veleda during the Batavian revolt.
bructeri.o: The Bructeri lived between the upper Ems and the Lippe, in what is now Westphalia. They appear in Roman sources from 12 BCE, when Drusus fought them on the Ems. In 9 CE they joined Arminius against Varus and captured the eagle of the Nineteenth Legion, which Germanicus' general Stertinius recovered in 15.
bructeri.r: Their leadership was in the hands of chiefs and an influential religious figure: the seeress Veleda, who lived in a tower near the Lippe, foretold the success of the Batavian revolt of 69 and was consulted by other peoples. Around 98, Tacitus reports that neighbouring tribes had nearly wiped out the Bructeri while Romans watched.
bructeri.e: The Bructeri survived that defeat and are mentioned again in the 4th century as part of the Franks. Their district, the Boructuari, was among the peoples evangelised by Saint Suitbert around 700, before the Saxons overran it.

bolognese-republic.t: The brief republic set up in Bologna in 1796 after the French expelled papal rule, which soon merged into the Cispadane Republic.
bolognese-republic.o: In June 1796 French troops entered Bologna, part of the Papal States, and the papal legate left. The city's Senate, under French protection, took over the government, and Bologna declared itself a free republic.
bolognese-republic.r: Bologna's old ruling families kept much of their influence, governing through the Senate and new committees while meeting French demands for money and art. The republic drafted a constitution in late 1796. It sent delegates to the congresses that united Bologna with Ferrara, Modena and Reggio.
bolognese-republic.e: By the end of 1796 Bologna had joined the Cispadane Republic, which in 1797 became part of the Cisalpine Republic.

beylik-of-mani.t: Semi-autonomous Ottoman principality of the Mani peninsula, whose last bey, Petrobey Mavromichalis, helped launch the Greek War of Independence.
beylik-of-mani.o: The Maniots of the southern Peloponnese had always resisted Ottoman control. After the failed Orlov revolt of 1770 and the Russo-Turkish peace of 1774, the Ottomans gave up direct rule and in 1776 created a Beylik of Mani under the authority of the Kapudan Pasha, the Ottoman admiral, with a Maniot bey.
beylik-of-mani.r: The bey, chosen from the Maniot clans, paid a modest tribute and kept order, but power remained with the feuding chieftain families in their stone tower houses. Notable beys included Tzanetos Grigorakis and, from 1815, Petros Mavromichalis. The Mani was poor, with olive oil, piracy and a strong warrior tradition shaping its society.
beylik-of-mani.e: In March 1821 Petrobey Mavromichalis declared revolt at Areopolis and Kalamata, joining the Greek War of Independence. The beylik ended, and the Mani became part of the First Hellenic Republic, though its clans long resisted central government.

billung-march.t: A Saxon frontier march facing the Obotrites along the lower Elbe, held by the Billung family until the great Slavic revolt of 1066.
billung-march.o: Around 936 Otto I entrusted Hermann Billung with command against the Slavs along the lower Elbe, from Holstein to the Peene. This frontier region, later called the Billung March, covered roughly modern Mecklenburg and eastern Holstein, inhabited mainly by Obotrites and other Wendish peoples who paid tribute.
billung-march.r: The march was less a settled territory than a zone of military overlordship and tribute collection. The Billungs, who also became dukes of Saxony, controlled it from strongholds along the Elbe. Bishoprics such as Oldenburg in Holstein were founded to convert the Slavs, but German control remained loose and the Obotrite princes kept considerable power.
billung-march.e: The Great Slav Rising of 983 shook German control, and after the murder of the Christian Obotrite prince Gottschalk in 1066 the Slavs expelled German influence and destroyed churches. The march ceased to exist; German rule returned only with Henry the Lion in the 12th century, leading to the Lordship of Mecklenburg.

burgundian-state.t: The patchwork realm of the Valois dukes of Burgundy, from Dijon to the North Sea, whose court set the fashion of 15th-century Europe.
burgundian-state.o: In 1363 John II of France gave the Duchy of Burgundy to his son Philip the Bold. Philip's marriage to Margaret of Male brought Flanders, Artois and the Free County of Burgundy in 1384. His grandson Philip the Good added Namur, Brabant, Holland, Zeeland, Hainaut and Luxembourg between 1421 and 1443.
burgundian-state.r: The dukes held their lands by different titles under France and the Empire and tried to bind them with common institutions, a Chamber of Accounts, the States General from 1464 and the Order of the Golden Fleece, founded in 1430. Flemish and Brabantine towns supplied wealth from cloth and trade, and painters such as Jan van Eyck and Rogier van der Weyden worked for the court.
burgundian-state.e: Charles the Bold sought a crown but was killed at Nancy in 1477. Louis XI seized the duchy; Mary of Burgundy married Maximilian of Austria, and after her death in 1482 the Treaty of Arras split the inheritance, the Low Countries passing to the Habsburg Netherlands.

balearica.t: The late Roman province of the Balearic Islands, separated from Carthaginiensis in the 4th century and lost to the Vandals in 455.
balearica.o: The Balearic Islands, conquered by Rome in 123 BCE, belonged to Hispania Citerior, Tarraconensis and then Carthaginiensis. Around 369 they became a separate province, Balearica, under a governor in the Diocese of Hispania.
balearica.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and trade, with towns such as Palma, Pollentia and on Menorca Mago and Iamo. Christianity was well established by the 5th century. A letter of Bishop Severus of Minorca describes the forced conversion of the Jews of Mago in 418, a rare window on island life.
balearica.e: Vandal raids from Africa struck the islands from 425. Around 455 the Vandals under Gaiseric took control, ending Roman rule. The islands passed to Byzantium after Belisarius' reconquest of Africa in 534.

barony-of-kalavryta.t: Short-lived Frankish barony in the mountains of northern Peloponnese, one of the first lost to the reviving Byzantines.
barony-of-kalavryta.o: Kalavryta was one of the twelve baronies set up in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Otho of Tournay and covered the mountainous district around the town of Kalavryta in the northern Peloponnese, with twelve knight's fiefs.
barony-of-kalavryta.r: Like other baronies, it was held by a French knightly family owing military service and counsel to the prince and governing a Greek peasant population from a castle. Records say little more about it than the name of its lords.
barony-of-kalavryta.e: After the Principality ceded Mistras and other forts to Byzantium in 1262, Byzantine forces pushed north. Kalavryta was taken around 1270 and the barony ceased to exist, though the area later changed hands again before passing permanently to the Despotate of the Morea.

bourbon-spain.t: Spain under the Bourbon dynasty from Philip V to Isabella II, a time of centralising reform, Napoleonic invasion and the loss of most of its American empire.
bourbon-spain.o: Charles II, last of Habsburg Spain, left the throne to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV, who became Philip V in 1700. The War of the Spanish Succession confirmed him as king but cost Spain its European possessions at Utrecht in 1713, while the Nueva Planta decrees abolished the separate institutions of the Crown of Aragon.
bourbon-spain.r: The Bourbons built a more centralised state on the French model, with intendants, new academies and royal factories. Charles III (1759-1788) promoted roads, trade reform and enlightened ministers and expelled the Jesuits. The monarchy was shattered by the 1808 French invasion; Ferdinand VII then restored absolutism, and the American colonies won independence in the 1810s and 1820s.
bourbon-spain.e: Isabella II's reign was dominated by Carlist Wars, generals and court scandal. The Glorious Revolution of September 1868 drove her into exile, opening the Sexenio Democrático.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern Andalusia, in modern Granada, Almería and Jaén, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was Basti, near Baza, and they bordered the Oretani, Contestani and coastal Bastuli.
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and Basti, where the Lady of Baza, a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under Rome during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between Hispania Citerior and Baetica in Roman times.

barcid-iberia.t: The Carthaginian domain built in Iberia by Hamilcar Barca and his heirs, the silver-rich base from which Hannibal set out to invade Italy.
barcid-iberia.o: After losing Sicily in the First Punic War, Carthage sent Hamilcar Barca to Iberia in 237 BCE. Landing at Gadir, he conquered the Guadalquivir valley and its mines. After his death in about 229 BCE, his son-in-law Hasdrubal extended Carthaginian power by diplomacy and founded Qart Hadasht, later Carthago Nova, around 227 BCE.
barcid-iberia.r: Barcid Iberia was run almost as a family dominion of the Barcids, nominally under Carthage. Silver from mines near Qart Hadasht and the Sierra Morena paid for armies of Iberian, Celtiberian and African troops. Alliances with local rulers were sealed by marriages, such as Hannibal's to Himilce of Castulo. In 226 BCE the Ebro treaty with Rome fixed a northern limit.
barcid-iberia.e: Hannibal, in command from 221 BCE, took Saguntum in 219 BCE, starting the Second Punic War. Scipio captured Qart Hadasht in 209 BCE and won at Ilipa in 206 BCE, ending Carthaginian rule. The territory became the Roman provinces of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.

barony-of-vostitsa.t: Barony of the Principality of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Vostitsa, the modern Aigio.
barony-of-vostitsa.o: After the Frankish conquest of the Peloponnese, the Principality of Achaea was divided into twelve baronies around 1209. Vostitsa, with a modest number of knight's fiefs, was granted to the Charpigny family from Burgundy, who held it through the 13th century.
barony-of-vostitsa.r: The barons held the castle and town on the south shore of the Gulf of Corinth, owed military service to the prince and sat in his high court, while Greek villagers farmed the land under them. Little detail of daily government survives beyond mentions in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin records.
barony-of-vostitsa.e: In the 14th century the barony passed by inheritance and sale among the Enghien and other lords, and became involved in the struggles of the Navarrese Company. It was eventually lost to the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea in the early 15th century, as the principality crumbled.

barony-of-patras.t: The largest barony of the Principality of Achaea, centred on the port of Patras, later sold to its Latin archbishop.
barony-of-patras.o: When the Principality of Achaea was organised around 1209, Patras, the main port of the north-western Peloponnese, was granted as a barony with 24 knight's fiefs to William Aleman, a knight possibly of German or Provencal origin. He fortified the ancient citadel above the town.
barony-of-patras.r: The barons held the castle and city, owed service to the prince and shared the town with the Latin archbishop, who was the senior Catholic prelate in the principality. Patras was a commercial centre for silk, currants and trade with Italy, with a Greek majority under Latin lords.
barony-of-patras.e: Over the 13th century the archbishops acquired the baronial rights. Around 1276 the barony passed to the archbishop, creating the Latin Archbishopric of Patras, a church-ruled state that lasted until 1430.

byzantine-spania.t: The East Roman foothold on Spain's south-east coast, won by Justinian in 552 and held for some seventy years against the Visigoths.
byzantine-spania.o: In 552 the Visigothic noble Athanagild, rebelling against King Agila, sought help from Justinian. An imperial force under the elderly patrician Liberius landed in the south-east, and in the following years the Byzantines seized a coastal strip from around Cartagena to Málaga and beyond, organised as the province of Spania.
byzantine-spania.r: Spania was run by a magister militum based at Carthago Nova, and an inscription of 589 records the governor Comenciolus repairing the city's defences. It formed part of Justinian's restoration of the Roman Empire in the West, linked to Byzantine Africa. Its population was Hispano-Roman and Catholic, and Byzantine authority was mainly military and fiscal.
byzantine-spania.e: Visigothic kings steadily pushed the Byzantines back. Leovigild retook inland areas, Sisebut captured Málaga around 615, and Suintila expelled the last imperial forces around 624. Carthago Nova was destroyed in the fighting.

bourbon-restoration.t: The return of the Bourbon kings after Napoleon, a constitutional monarchy under Louis XVIII and Charles X that ended in the July Revolution of 1830.
bourbon-restoration.o: After Napoleon's abdication in April 1814 the allies and the French Senate restored Louis XVIII, brother of Louis XVI. He granted the Charter of 1814, which kept a parliament and many revolutionary gains. Napoleon's return in the Hundred Days of 1815 interrupted the regime until Waterloo.
bourbon-restoration.r: France had a two-chamber parliament elected by a very small, wealthy electorate. Moderate ministers such as the Duke of Richelieu paid off war indemnities and ended the allied occupation in 1818, while ultra-royalists pressed for revenge after the White Terror. Charles X, crowned at Reims in 1825, compensated émigrés and favoured the Church.
bourbon-restoration.e: In July 1830 Charles X issued ordinances dissolving parliament and curbing the press. Three days of revolt in Paris drove him into exile, and Louis-Philippe of Orléans became king, beginning the July Monarchy. Algiers had been taken weeks earlier.

bruttii.t: Oscan-speaking people who broke away from the Lucanians in 356 BCE and dominated the toe of Italy, Hannibal's last stronghold.
bruttii.o: Diodorus says that in 356 BCE runaway slaves and herdsmen in the mountains of Calabria, then under Lucanian control, rebelled and formed a new people, the Bruttii. The story may simplify a revolt of a subject population, but by the late 4th century BCE they were an independent federation.
bruttii.r: Their capital was Consentia (Cosenza). They lived in hill towns and drew wealth from the Sila forest, producing pitch and timber. They captured Greek cities including Hipponion and Terina and minted fine coins. They fought Alexander of Epirus and joined Pyrrhus against Rome.
bruttii.e: Rome subdued them by 270 BCE and took half the Sila. They joined Hannibal after Cannae, and Bruttium was his last base in Italy until he left in 203 BCE. As punishment they lost land and status; Roman writers said they were reduced to serving as attendants to magistrates.

bosporan-kingdom.t: Long-lived Greek kingdom on the Kerch Strait that fed Athens with Black Sea grain and survived as a Roman client state until the coming of the Huns.
bosporan-kingdom.o: Greek colonies on both sides of the Cimmerian Bosporus, such as Panticapaeum, Phanagoria and Theodosia, united under the Archaeanactid dynasty around 480 BCE. In 438 BCE power passed to Spartocus I, whose Spartocid descendants ruled for more than three centuries from Panticapaeum, modern Kerch, extending control over local Sindians and Maeotians.
bosporan-kingdom.r: The Spartocids called themselves archons of the Greek cities and kings of the native peoples. Wealth came from grain, fish and slaves shipped to the Aegean: Leucon I (389-349 BCE) granted Athens tax-free grain purchases and was honoured there. Rich kurgan burials show a blend of Greek and Scythian and Sarmatian culture.
bosporan-kingdom.e: Under pressure from the Scythians, Paerisades V handed the kingdom to Mithridates VI of Pontus c. 108 BCE. Later kings, such as Aspurgus and his successors, ruled as clients of Rome. The kingdom declined in the 3rd century CE and was overrun by the Huns in the 370s.
bosporan-kingdom.re: Ancient Greek religion, later also Christianity and Judaism

bibroci.t: British people named only once by Julius Caesar, among the groups that surrendered to him during his second invasion in 54 BCE.
bibroci.o: Known only from Caesar's Gallic War, the Bibroci were one of five British peoples, with the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Ancalites and Cassi, who sent envoys to surrender to him in 54 BCE after the Trinovantes had come under his protection.
bibroci.r: Nothing is recorded of their government, rulers or way of life. Their territory is unknown; scholars have suggested places in the Thames valley or in Berkshire and Sussex, but no inscription or coin securely names them.
bibroci.e: They vanish from the record after Caesar's account. Their land was presumably absorbed by larger neighbours such as the Atrebates (Britain) or the Catuvellauni before the Roman conquest of 43.

banu-ghaniya-majorca.t: The last Almoravid state, ruled from Majorca by the Banu Ghaniya, who waged a long war against the Almohads from the Balearics to Ifriqiya.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.o: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Ghaniya, of an Almoravid family related to the ruling dynasty, governed the Balearic Islands from about 1126. When the Almoravid Empire collapsed in the 1140s, he kept the islands as an independent emirate loyal to the Abbasid caliph.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.r: Under Ishaq ibn Muhammad (c. 1155-1183) Majorca prospered on trade and corsair raids, and made treaties with Genoa and Pisa. In 1184 Ali ibn Ghaniya invaded North Africa, seizing Bejaia and starting a war against the Almohads in Ifriqiya that lasted half a century.
banu-ghaniya-majorca.e: The Almohads conquered Majorca in 1203, killing its ruler Abd Allah ibn Ishaq, though the family fought on in Ifriqiya. James I of Aragon took Majorca in 1229, later forming the Kingdom of Majorca.

barony-of-passavant.t: Frankish barony in the Mani held by the marshals of Achaea, whose castle of Passava watched over the unruly Maniots.
barony-of-passavant.o: Around 1220 John of Neuilly, hereditary marshal of the Principality of Achaea, received a fief at the entrance to the Mani peninsula and built a castle there called Passavant, now Passava, near Gytheio. Its purpose was to control the independent-minded population of the Mani and the route into Laconia.
barony-of-passavant.r: The barony was small but held by one of the great officers of the principality, the marshal, who commanded the army. Its lords ruled from the castle over Greek villages, alongside the castle of Grand Magne built by William II of Villehardouin further south.
barony-of-passavant.e: After William II was captured at Pelagonia in 1259, he ceded Mistras, Monemvasia and Grand Magne to Byzantium, and Passavant was lost to the Byzantines soon after, around 1263. The Neuilly heiress Margaret of Passavant later claimed Akova.

belegezites.t: Slavic tribe settled in Thessaly in the 7th century, remembered for trading grain with besieged Thessalonica.
belegezites.o: The Belegezites were one of the Slavic groups that settled in the Balkans during the great migrations of the late 6th and 7th centuries. They occupied lands in Thessaly around Phthiotic Thebes and Demetrias on the Gulf of Volos. Almost everything known about them comes from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius, a Byzantine collection of stories about Thessalonica.
belegezites.r: They lived as farming communities under their own chiefs, partly independent of Byzantium. During the Slavic siege of Thessalonica in the 670s they did not join the attackers but sold grain to the starving city, a sign of their prosperity and pragmatic relations with the Byzantines. Their name survives in later Byzantine sources as the region of Velegezitia.
belegezites.e: Over the 8th and 9th centuries Byzantium reasserted control over Greece through the theme system, and the Belegezites were gradually brought under imperial administration, converted to Christianity and absorbed into the Greek-speaking population. They leave few traces apart from place names.
belegezites.re: Slavic paganism, later Eastern Orthodox Christianity

barony-of-chalandritsa.t: Small Frankish barony in the hills south of Patras, one of the original fiefs of the Principality of Achaea.
barony-of-chalandritsa.o: Chalandritsa was among the baronies created in the Principality of Achaea around 1209. It was granted to Robert de la Tremouille, a knight from France, and held a small number of knight's fiefs in the hill country of Achaea south of Patras.
barony-of-chalandritsa.r: The barons owed military service to the prince and had seats in his high court. The Dramelay family later held it for much of the 13th and 14th centuries. Beyond these facts, recorded in the Chronicle of the Morea and Angevin documents, little is known of the barony's internal life.
barony-of-chalandritsa.e: In the final collapse of the principality, Chalandritsa was taken by the Byzantines of the Despotate of the Morea, under Constantine Palaiologos, in 1429, at the same time as the campaign that won Patras.

banu-qasi.t: A Muslim dynasty of Visigothic descent that dominated the upper Ebro for two centuries, allied by blood with the kings of Pamplona.
banu-qasi.o: The Banu Qasi claimed descent from a Visigothic count called Cassius who converted to Islam after the conquest of 711 to 714, keeping his lands in the upper Ebro valley. As muwallads, native Muslims, they became the leading family of the Upper March, based at Tudela.
banu-qasi.r: They balanced between Córdoba, the Franks and the Christian kingdoms, intermarrying with the Arista family of Pamplona, whose founder Íñigo Arista was a half-brother of Musa ibn Musa. Musa ruled Tudela, Zaragoza and Huesca and was called the third king of Spain, until Ordoño I of Asturias defeated him at Albelda in 859. Later family members fought Córdoba, the Tujibids and Navarre.
banu-qasi.e: Weakened by family divisions and wars with Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona, the dynasty lost Tudela and its lands. Abd al-Rahman III ended its power in the 920s, and the Tujibid family took over the Upper March.

byzantium.t: Megarian colony on the Bosporus that controlled the passage to the Black Sea and later became Constantinople.
byzantium.o: Settlers from Megara, led according to tradition by Byzas, founded Byzantium c. 667 BCE on the European promontory between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara. The site commanded the Bosporus, the only sea route between the Aegean and the Black Sea.
byzantium.r: Byzantium grew rich from tuna fishing and tolls on shipping, especially the grain trade. It came under the Achaemenid Empire, was taken by the Spartan regent Pausanias in 478 BCE and then joined the Delian League, revolting in 440 BCE. Its resistance to Philip II's siege of 340 to 339 BCE was celebrated. In 220 BCE Rhodes went to war over its new tolls.
byzantium.e: Byzantium allied with Rome in the 2nd century BCE and kept its freedom until Vespasian brought it into a Roman province c. 73 CE. Constantine refounded it as Constantinople in 330 CE, capital of the Byzantine Empire.

bigerriones.t: Aquitanian people of the high Pyrenean valleys around Tarbes, who gave their name to Bigorre.
bigerriones.o: The Bigerriones lived in the upper Adour valley and the Pyrenean foothills of the modern Hautes-Pyrénées. Caesar lists them among the Aquitanian peoples who surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE.
bigerriones.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Like other Aquitani they spoke a language related to Basque, and their economy combined mountain herding with farming in the valleys.
bigerriones.e: Under Rome their chief town was Turba, later Tarbes, within the province of Aquitania and then Novempopulana. Their name passed to the medieval County of Bigorre.

brigantes-ireland.t: People of south-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, bearing the same name as the great Brigantes confederation of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 lists the Brigantes in south-eastern Ireland, usually placed in the area of modern Wexford and Waterford, near the Coriondi and the Usdiae. The name, meaning roughly 'the high ones' or linked to the goddess Brigantia, is the same as that of the Brigantes of northern Britain.
brigantes-ireland.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. The shared name has encouraged theories of migration from Britain to Ireland, or of a common cult of a goddess later remembered as Brigit, but there is no evidence beyond the name. The south-east coast faced Wales and Gaul and was open to sea trade.
brigantes-ireland.e: The Irish Brigantes vanish from the record after Ptolemy. Their area later lay within the Kingdom of Leinster, the Kingdom of Osraige and the lands of the Deisi Muman.

broerec.t: Breton kingdom of the Vannes region, named the land of Waroch after a warlord who defied the Franks.
broerec.o: In the 6th century Breton rulers extended their power over the Vannetais, the former land of the Veneti, which remained largely Gallo-Roman. Gregory of Tours records the counts Macliau and his son Waroch fighting for control of Vannes.
broerec.r: Waroch repeatedly raided Frankish territory around Rennes and Nantes and defeated or bought off Frankish armies sent by Guntram and Chilperic I in the 570s and 580s. The region kept a strong Gallo-Roman element alongside the Breton settlers, and Vannes remained a bishopric.
broerec.e: Broërec remained the border zone between the Bretons and the Franks until it was absorbed into the Kingdom of Brittany created by Nominoe, who was count of Vannes for Louis the Pious. Its name survives in the Breton name of the Vannes region.

batavian-republic.t: The Dutch revolutionary republic set up with French help in 1795, which created the first unitary Dutch state and a modern constitution.
batavian-republic.o: In January 1795 French armies crossed the frozen rivers into the Dutch Republic, and stadtholder William V fled to England. Dutch Patriots, exiled since 1787, proclaimed the Batavian Republic, named after the ancient Batavians. The Treaty of The Hague bound it to France and imposed a heavy indemnity.
batavian-republic.r: After fierce debate a constitution of 1798 replaced the old federation with a unitary state, separated church and state and gave Jews equal rights. Coups followed in 1798 and 1801. The fleet was destroyed at Camperdown in 1797, colonies were lost to Britain, and trade suffered. In 1805 Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck became Grand Pensionary with wide powers.
batavian-republic.e: Napoleon, wanting firmer control, turned the republic into the Kingdom of Holland in 1806 under his brother Louis Bonaparte. Its administrative reforms, national taxes and codified law survived into the later Kingdom of the Netherlands.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the Jalón and Huerva valleys of modern Zaragoza province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included Segeda and Contrebia Belaisca, the modern Botorrita.
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The Botorrita bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from Contrebia Belaisca and record local regulations, while a Latin bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE Segeda enlarged its walls, which Rome treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by Carus of Segeda, the Celtiberians defeated the consul Nobilior, but after Numantia fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of Boeotia shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE Thebes was gathering them into a federation, an effort Plataea resisted by allying with Athens. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of Athens at Coronea in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia describes its 5th-century constitution: Boeotia was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with Thebes holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The King's Peace dissolved it in 386 BCE, but Pelopidas and Epaminondas revived it after 379 BCE and defeated Sparta at Leuctra. Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until Rome dissolved it in 171 BCE.

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the Pennines and northern England, from the Mersey and Humber to the Tyne. Their name is linked to the goddess Brigantia. By the time of the Roman invasion of 43 they were under the rule of Queen Cartimandua, who made a treaty with Rome and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. Cartimandua handed the fugitive Caratacus to the Romans in 51, and later her divorce from her consort Venutius split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 Venutius drove Cartimandua out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. Petillius Cerialis then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at York. The southern territory became a civitas centred on Isurium Brigantum, Aldborough, in Roman Britain.

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of Iberia, roughly from the Strait of Gibraltar to Almería, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as Malaka, Sexi and Abdera.
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under Hispania Ulterior and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into Baetica.

bailiwick-of-jersey.t: The largest Channel Island, a self-governing Crown Dependency that has stayed loyal to the English crown since the loss of Normandy in 1204.
bailiwick-of-jersey.o: Jersey was part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. After King John lost mainland Normandy in 1204, the island remained with the English crown and became a separate bailiwick under a warden, later a lieutenant governor, with a bailiff heading its Royal Court.
bailiwick-of-jersey.r: Jersey kept Norman customary law and its own States assembly. Mont Orgueil Castle defended it against frequent French attacks. The island traded in cod from Newfoundland, knitted woollens and later potatoes and cattle, and grew into a financial centre. Charles II was proclaimed king there in 1649, and the French were defeated at the Battle of Jersey in 1781.
bailiwick-of-jersey.e: Germany occupied Jersey from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency outside the United Kingdom, with its own parliament, the States Assembly, and its own laws and taxes.

bastarnae.t: Probably Germanic people of the lower Danube and Carpathians who fought for Macedon against Rome and later joined the Goths.
bastarnae.o: The Bastarnae appeared north of the lower Danube around 200 BCE, the first Germanic-speaking people known to Greek and Roman writers, though some ancient authors thought them Celts. One branch, the Peucini, lived on the island of Peuce in the Danube delta.
bastarnae.r: They were a warlike confederation of tribes, valued as mercenaries. Philip V and Perseus of Macedon recruited them against Rome, and the Zarubintsy and Poienești-Lukashevka archaeological cultures are often linked to them. In 62 BCE they defeated Gaius Antonius Hybrida near Histria. In 29 BCE Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated them and killed their king Deldo in single combat.
bastarnae.e: Under the empire they remained a frontier people, joining the Goths and Carpi in 3rd-century raids. Around 280 the emperor Probus settled a large number of Bastarnae in Thrace, after which they disappear as a distinct people.
